posts.title: What is SEWA AI? The clinical intelligence platform explained
posts.subtitle: A complete walkthrough of the platform, from DICOM ingestion to clinical report
posts.excerpt: SEWA AI is a trust-first clinical imaging platform that triages and prioritises critical radiology findings. This post explains exactly how it works — from the moment a scan arrives to the moment a radiologist acts.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.cta: See the platform in action → book a demo
posts.content:
The problem SEWA was built to solve

Every day, thousands of chest X-rays, CT head scans, CT chest scans, and CT angiograms arrive in NHS radiology departments with the same anxious question: is there something urgent here, and has anyone noticed it? The stakes could not be higher. An undetected intracranial haemorrhage, a missed pulmonary embolism, an unnoticed pneumothorax — each represents a window in which clinical intervention could have changed the outcome.

SEWA AI is a clinical imaging intelligence platform designed to triage and prioritise these time-critical findings, automatically flagging urgent studies and routing them to the top of the radiologist's worklist. But SEWA is not just another detection tool. It is a complete clinical intelligence platform — from DICOM ingestion through AI inference, uncertainty quantification, hallucination screening, human sign-off, and reporting — built around one architectural principle: knowing when you do not know is as important as knowing what you do.

How SEWA works: the end-to-end pipeline

SEWA's pipeline processes a clinical scan through a series of interconnected stages, each designed to address a distinct failure mode in clinical AI. The platform currently covers adult thoracic and acute radiology — chest X-ray, CT head, CT chest, and CTA — with a modular architecture that allows additional modalities to be added without redesigning the core safety layers.

Stage 1: DICOM ingestion and pre-processing

When a DICOM study arrives — whether from a PACS system, a local workstation, or a Go DICOM edge device — SEWA ingests the series, normalises the pixel data, and prepares it for inference. The pre-processing pipeline handles common artefacts, checks series completeness, and flags studies that do not meet the expected protocol. Every step is logged, creating an audit trail from the moment the scan enters the system.

Stage 2: AI inference with uncertainty decomposition

The inference engine runs the study through a family of deep-learning models trained on thoracic and acute radiology. Rather than returning a single confidence score, each model returns an uncertainty decomposition — separating aleatoric uncertainty (noise inherent in the image data) from epistemic uncertainty (the model's own knowledge limitations). This decomposition is the foundation of SEWA's entire safety architecture.

Stage 3: The Metacognition Gate

Before any finding is dispatched to a clinician, the Metacognition Engine checks the output against anatomical, physiological, and contextual constraints. If the model proposes a finding that is inconsistent with the patient's demographics, the imaging modality, or basic clinical logic — or if its uncertainty is too high to make a reliable recommendation — the finding is flagged for deeper review rather than dispatched. The engine catches 96.3% of hallucinations in internal testing (n=500).

Stage 4: Database-layer human sign-off

A SEWA finding never becomes an approved clinical result unless a consultant radiologist has explicitly accepted it at the database layer. There is no UI prompt the user can dismiss, no administrator override, and no bypass path. Human oversight is structural — enforced by the data model itself, not by a workflow setting.

Stage 5: Reporting and handoff

Once signed off, the finding — along with its uncertainty decomposition, hallucination-gate status, and sign-off record — is available in the reporting workflow. The platform generates structured findings that integrate with existing radiology information systems, ensuring that SEWA augments rather than replaces the clinical workflow.

What makes SEWA different

The differentiators are architectural, not cosmetic. Most clinical AI platforms offer a detection score and a notification. SEWA offers a complete trust stack: uncertainty quantification, a hallucination gate, non-bypassable sign-off, and offline continuity — each addressing a documented reason that NHS AI adoption stalls. The platform is UK-sovereign, zero-PHI-egress, and designed for both cloud and edge deployment.

SEWA is at Technology Readiness Level 5 (TRL 5), with internal engineering results including an AUC-ROC of 0.961 (n=14,200) and a catch rate of 96.3% (n=500). These are engineering tests, not clinical validation — and they are presented as such. The path to clinical evidence runs through a prospective shadow trial, an NIHR EME application, and ultimately UKCA Class IIb certification (planned Q2 2027).

A platform built for the NHS

SEWA was designed for the NHS environment from the ground up. It is listed on G-Cloud 14, meaning NHS Trusts can deploy it in under five business days without a competitive tender. It complies with NHS DSPT and GDPR requirements. It aligns with DCB0129 and DCB0160 governance standards. And it is built to work in environments where connectivity is unreliable — an edge deployment that runs on under 20 MB of RAM and syncs to the cloud when the network resumes.

posts.title: How SEWA's Uncertainty Engine quantifies what it does not know
posts.subtitle: Most clinical AI gives a single confidence score. SEWA tells you when it is uncertain.
posts.excerpt: In clinical AI, a confidence score without uncertainty quantification is incomplete. A model that is 60% confident is not 60% certain — it may be guessing. SEWA's Uncertainty Engine decomposes predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistatic components, surfacing cases where the model's knowledge is thin so they receive deeper review.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.cta: Read the full competitive landscape report →
posts.content:
Why a single confidence score is not enough

Nearly every clinical AI platform reports a confidence score. A finding is flagged and accompanied by a number — often between 0 and 1, sometimes as a percentage. This score tells you how strongly the model's weights align with the label in its training data. It does not tell you whether the model is certain.

This distinction matters enormously in clinical settings. Consider two scenarios. In the first, a model is 95% confident that a chest X-ray shows a large pleural effusion — and it does. In the second, a model is 60% confident that a scan shows a small pneumothorax at the lung apex — an area notoriously difficult to read, even for experienced radiologists. Both are presented identically by platforms that report only a confidence score. But the second case is far more dangerous, because the model's uncertainty signals that its knowledge of this particular finding is thin.

SEWA's Uncertainty Engine addresses this by decomposing predictive uncertainty into two components:

  • Aleatoric uncertainty — the noise inherent in the input data. Image quality, artefacts, patient positioning, and anatomical variation all contribute aleatoric uncertainty. A noisy, poorly positioned X-ray carries higher aleatoric uncertainty than a clean, well-positioned one.
  • Epistemic uncertainty — the model's own knowledge limitations. This captures when the model is operating outside its training distribution: a finding it has rarely seen, an anatomy it does not know well, or a combination of features it has not learned to interpret reliably.

By separating these two sources of uncertainty, SEWA can answer a more nuanced question than "how confident am I?" — it can answer "what kind of uncertainty am I facing, and what should I do about it?"

How the Uncertainty Engine works in practice

The Uncertainty Engine runs alongside the primary inference models. For each study, it produces:

  1. A primary finding — the detected abnormality, its location, and its estimated acuity.
  2. An uncertainty decomposition — aleatoric and epistatic components, each quantified.
  3. A risk tier — derived from the combination of finding severity and uncertainty level, determining whether the study is routed for immediate review, standard review, or deeper analysis.

Studies with high epistemic uncertainty — where the model knows it does not know — are automatically routed for deeper analysis or flagged for radiologist review with an explicit uncertainty notice. This ensures that cases where the model's knowledge is thin receive the human attention they deserve, rather than being dismissed as a low-confidence alert or, worse, being trusted implicitly.

Why this matters for patient safety

The clinical harm from AI in radiology comes in two forms. The first is false positives — alerts that trigger unnecessary procedures, contributing to alert fatigue and eroding radiologist trust in AI tools. The second is false negatives — findings the model misses entirely, or misses because it was uncertain but did not signal that uncertainty. Uncertainty quantification addresses both: by surfacing uncertainty, SEWA reduces false positives (low-confidence alerts are not dispatched) and mitigates false negatives (high-uncertainty cases are flagged for review).

This is not a theoretical benefit. Alert fatigue is one of the most frequently cited reasons that NHS AI adoption stalls. When clinicians are bombarded with low-quality alerts, they learn to ignore them — and the patients who most need an AI second pair of eyes are the ones who fall through the gap. By quantifying uncertainty and routing only high-quality signals to the clinical workflow, SEWA is designed to break this cycle.

posts.title: Metacognition in clinical AI: how SEWA catches its own hallucinations
posts.subtitle: Large language models hallucinate — and so can clinical AI. The Metacognition Engine intercepts them before they reach a clinician.
posts.excerpt: When an AI system confidently states a finding that is not present, that is a hallucination. In radiology, a hallucinated pulmonary embolism triggers an unnecessary CT pulmonary angiogram; a missed pneumothorax delays treatment. SEWA's Metacognition Engine catches 96.3% of hallucinations in internal testing, acting as a pre-dispatch gate that checks every output against anatomical and physiological constraints before it is ever shown to a clinician.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.content:
What is a hallucination in clinical AI?

A hallucination in clinical AI occurs when the system produces an output that is confidently presented as a finding but is not supported by the input data. Unlike a random error, a hallucination is plausible — it looks like a real finding, uses the correct medical terminology, and is often accompanied by a high confidence score. This is precisely what makes it dangerous.

In radiology, a hallucinated finding can trigger a cascade of clinical actions: a false-positive pulmonary embolism leads to an unnecessary CT pulmonary angiogram with contrast, an incidental finding of a non-existent aortic dissection prompts an emergency workup, a hallucinated pneumothorax results in an unnecessary chest drain. Each intervention carries its own risk, and each erodes the clinician's trust in the AI tools they are asked to adopt.

Less visibly, hallucinations in the opposite direction are equally concerning — real findings that are suppressed because the model is uncertain but does not signal that uncertainty. A missed pneumothorax, a delayed intracranial haemorrhage, a forgotten pulmonary embolism. In time-critical radiology, a delayed finding is often as dangerous as a false one.

Both directions of hallucination are patient-safety problems, and both stem from the same root cause: the model's inability to know the limits of its own knowledge.

Why clinical AI hallucinates

Hallucinations in clinical AI arise from several sources. First, training distribution mismatch: when a model encounters an anatomy, pathology, or imaging artefact it has not learned to interpret, it may still produce an output — but one that is not grounded in the input. Second, adversarial or noisy inputs: subtle artefacts, patient movement, or technical variations can push a model towards spurious correlations. Third, overconfidence: many models are calibrated to produce high-confidence outputs even when the input falls outside their reliable range.

The common thread is that the model is not signalling its own uncertainty. A hallucination is not a random mistake — it is a confident assertion built on thin or absent evidence. Catching it requires a system that does not just ask "what do I see?" but "how sure am I that what I see is real?"

The Metacognition Engine: a pre-dispatch hallucination gate

SEWA's Metacognition Engine is a pre-dispatch hallucination gate that checks every AI output against anatomical, physiological, and contextual constraints before it is ever shown to a clinician. Rather than relying on a single confidence threshold, the engine applies a multi-layered consistency check:

  1. Anatomical plausibility — does the proposed finding correspond to a real anatomical structure in the scanned region? A pulmonary embolism in the leg, or a hepatic lesion in the lung, fails this check.
  2. Physiological consistency — is the finding consistent with what is physiologically plausible for this patient? An incidental finding of a pathology that would have produced detectable symptoms in an asymptomatic patient is flagged.
  3. Uncertainty thresholding — if the epistemic uncertainty exceeds a defined threshold, the finding is routed for deeper analysis rather than dispatched, regardless of its apparent severity.
  4. Cross-modal consistency — when multiple findings are detected, are they mutually consistent? A reported pneumothorax alongside a reported pleural effusion in the same hemithorax, for example, may trigger a consistency review.

In internal testing against a curated set of hallucination cases, the Metacognition Engine caught 96.3% of hallucinations before they reached a clinician (n=500). The remaining 3.7% are flagged for ongoing model refinement.

Metacognition as a clinical safety principle

Metacognition — the ability to think about one's own thinking — is a skill that human clinicians develop over years of training and practice. An experienced radiologist knows when a scan is difficult to interpret and will recommend additional imaging or a second opinion. SEWA's Metacognition Engine encodes this same principle into the platform: the AI knows when it does not know, and acts accordingly.

This is not a replacement for clinical judgment — it is a complement. The Metacognition Gate ensures that the cases most in need of human expertise are the ones that receive it, while reducing the noise of false positives that contributes to alert fatigue. The result is a clinical workflow where AI-assisted reading is safer, more trustworthy, and more likely to be adopted.

posts.title: The SEWA safety architecture: uncertainty, hallucination gate, and non-bypassable sign-off
posts.subtitle: Three layers, each addressing a distinct failure mode in clinical AI
posts.excerpt: SEWA's safety architecture is built from three stacked layers. The Uncertainty Engine quantifies what the model knows and does not know. The Metacognition Gate checks for hallucinations and physiologically impossible outputs. And the database-layer sign-off enforces mandatory human review that cannot be bypassed, archived, or overridden.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.cta: Read the full report on SEWA's differentiation →
posts.content:
Why a single safety layer is not enough

Clinical AI can fail in multiple ways, and each failure mode requires a different countermeasure. A confidence threshold catches some false positives but not hallucinations. A hallucination gate catches implausible outputs but not cases where the model is simply uncertain. A human review step catches clinical errors but can be bypassed if it sits at the user interface level rather than the data layer.

SEWA's safety architecture addresses each failure mode with a dedicated layer, stacked so that the output of one layer feeds into the next. The architecture is not a collection of features — it is a unified safety stack where each layer addresses a distinct way clinical AI can fail.

Layer 1: Uncertainty decomposition

The Uncertainty Engine separates aleatoric uncertainty (noise inherent in the image data) from epistemic uncertainty (the model's knowledge limitations). High epistemic uncertainty signals that the model is operating outside its reliable range, and such cases are routed for deeper analysis or radiologist review rather than dispatched automatically.

Layer 2: The Metacognition Gate

Every output passes through the Metacognition Gate before dispatch. The gate checks anatomical plausibility, physiological consistency, uncertainty thresholds, and cross-modal consistency. In internal testing against a curated set of hallucination cases, the gate caught 96.3% of hallucinations before they reached a clinician (n=500).

Layer 3: Database-layer sign-off

A SEWA finding never becomes an approved clinical result unless a consultant radiologist has explicitly accepted it at the database layer. There is no UI prompt the user can dismiss, no administrator override, and no bypass path. Human oversight is structural — enforced by the data model itself.

How the layers work together

The three layers address distinct failure modes and together provide coverage that no single layer can offer alone. Uncertainty decomposition reduces false positives by routing low-confidence alerts. The Metacognition Gate catches hallucinations and implausible outputs. Database-layer sign-off ensures that no automated finding reaches a patient's care pathway without a clinician's explicit decision.

This is not a collection of features. It is a safety architecture designed from first principles to answer the documented reasons that NHS AI adoption stalls — alert fatigue, opaque single scores, bypassable oversight, and thin real-world evidence.

posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.content:
The connectivity problem

Clinical AI is typically assumed to run in the cloud — a central server processing studies as they arrive. For well-resourced NHS Trusts with resilient networks, this assumption holds. But for hospitals in low-connectivity settings, a cloud-only architecture is a barrier, not a solution. In parts of sub-Saharan Africa, 70% of hospitals cannot rely on consistent internet connectivity. A platform that requires a constant cloud connection cannot serve these settings.

SEWA was designed for this reality from the start. The edge deployment uses INT8-quantised models that run on under 20 MB of RAM, operates completely offline, and syncs to the cloud only when connectivity resumes. The same safety architecture — uncertainty decomposition, hallucination gating, and non-bypassable sign-off — applies whether the platform is online or offline.

70% of African hospitals cannot rely on consistent internet; Go DICOM service

The problem with UI-level review

Most clinical AI platforms place human review at the user interface level — a prompt the radiologist can dismiss, a modal they can close, a workflow they can override. In high-pressure clinical environments, these UI-level safeguards are frequently bypassed. A radiologist reading 200 studies in a shift does not want to stop and approve every AI notification. The result is a system that is designed to require human oversight but is engineered to allow it to be skipped.

SEWA takes a different approach. Sign-off is enforced at the database layer: a finding is never persisted as an approved clinical result unless a consultant radiologist has explicitly accepted it. There is no UI prompt the user can dismiss, no administrator override, and no bypass path. Human oversight is structural — enforced by the data model itself, not by a workflow setting.

posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.content:
What would a trust architecture require?

The clinical imaging AI market has produced well-funded, FDA-cleared, evidence-backed products. None has publicly delivered a complete trust architecture — a stack of complementary safety layers that each address a distinct failure mode, working together to cover the full spectrum of clinical AI risks.

A trust architecture in clinical AI requires at minimum four components. First, uncertainty quantification — the model must signal when its knowledge is thin, not just when it is confident. Second, hallucination gating — a pre-dispatch check that catches implausible or unsupported outputs before they reach a clinician. Third, non-bypassable human sign-off — ensuring that no automated finding reaches a patient's care pathway without a clinician's explicit decision. Fourth, offline continuity — the platform must function in low-connectivity settings without compromising safety.

Who is in the market?

The clinical imaging AI market is well-funded and growing fast. Harrison.ai, Qure.ai, Viz.ai, Brainomix, Lunit, and DeepHealth/Kheiron each hold regulatory clearances and published clinical studies. This post maps the landscape and frames where SEWA fits.

Harrison.ai leads in chest X-ray triage, with FDA clearance and deployment across more than 130 hospitals. Qure.ai has the largest regulatory footprint in tuberculosis screening, with FDA 510(k) clearance for qXR-Detect. Lunit holds regulatory clearance in South Korea and the US for lung and breast cancer screening. DeepHealth/Kheiron's GEMINI study, published in Nature Cancer in March 2026, demonstrated a 10.4% increase in cancer detection with over 30% workload reduction.

posts.content:
A crowded market with a missing ingredient

Clinical imaging AI is crowded with well-funded detection tools — Harrison.ai, Qure.ai, Viz.ai, Brainomix, Lunit, DeepHealth/Kheiron. Each has regulatory clearances and, in most cases, published clinical studies. But none has publicly delivered a complete trust architecture — uncertainty decomposition, hallucination gating, non-bypassable sign-off, and offline continuity, together in one platform.

The NHS already uses AI at scale — at least 54% of radiology departments use AI tools (RCR 2023) — and funds it through the AI in Health and Care Award and the AI Diagnostic Fund. But adoption still stalls on alert fatigue, opaque single scores, bypassable oversight, cloud-only outages, and thin real-world evidence.

Why detection alone is not enough

A detection tool tells you what it sees. A trustworthy AI platform tells you what it sees, how certain it is, whether what it sees makes physiological sense, and ensures a human decision-maker has explicitly accepted the finding before it reaches a patient. These are not incremental features — they address the documented reasons that NHS AI adoption stalls.

SEWA's differentiation is architectural and safety-led. It is designed from first principles to answer the documented reasons that NHS AI adoption fails. Its challenge is not identity — it is proof.

posts.title: The evidence pathway: from shadow trial to NIHR EME to UKCA Class IIb
posts.subtitle: A transparent roadmap for converting an architecturally differentiated platform into regulated, evidenced, deployed reality
posts.excerpt: SEWA's challenge is not identity — it is proof. The roadmap is deliberate: shadow trial → NIHR EME → UKCA Class IIb (Q2 2027). Each phase builds the independent clinical validation the market demands.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.content:
SEWA's challenge is proof, not identity

SEWA's differentiation is real and defensible. The differentiators mean nothing without independent validation. The roadmap is deliberate: a prospective shadow trial — 6 months, primary endpoint door-to-alert under 5 minutes — feeds into an NIHR EME application, which in turn supports a UKCA Class IIb submission (Q2 2027). Each phase is designed to build the evidence bar set by Brainomix's Lancet study and DeepHealth's GEMINI study.

Phase 1: Shadow trial

A prospective, 6-month study in an NHS partner Trust, comparing AI-assisted triage against standard reporting for time-critical findings. The primary endpoint is door-to-alert time under 5 minutes. Secondary endpoints include detection rate, false-positive rate, and radiologist satisfaction. The shadow trial does not replace clinical judgment — it augments it and generates the real-world evidence needed for regulatory submission.

Phase 2: NIHR EME

The Evidence and Evaluation programme funds rigorous independent assessment of health and care innovations. An NIHR EME application would subject SEWA's safety architecture and clinical performance to peer-reviewed evaluation — the same bar that Brainomix cleared with its Lancet publication.

Phase 3: UKCA Class IIb (Q2 2027)

With shadow trial data and NIHR evaluation in hand, SEWA would pursue UKCA Class IIb certification via the Notified Body pathway, aligned with MHRA's 2025 reform package and the UKCA marking route for innovative AI-based SaMD.

posts.subtitle: Public and Patient Involvement and Engagement is core to the research design
posts.excerpt: SEWA's clinical validation is built on PPIE from day one. The research programme, supported by the NIHR Research Delivery Network, includes patient advisory panels and NHS clinical leads across multiple regions.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
posts.content:
PPIE is not an add-on — it is the foundation

SEWA's clinical validation is built on Public and Patient Involvement and Engagement (PPIE) from day one. The research programme, supported by the NIHR Research Delivery Network, includes patient advisory panels, NHS clinical leads across multiple regions, and a governance framework that meets NIHR expectations.

How the research programme is structured

The programme is designed to be open, transparent, and aligned with NIHR standards. Clinical sites are selected to represent a diversity of NHS settings — from major academic teaching hospitals to district general trusts — ensuring the evidence generated is generalisable across the NHS. Patient advisory panels shape the study design, endpoint selection, and patient-facing materials.

How partners and research sites can join

Partnerships are welcome at every stage — from co-developing the research protocol to providing clinical sites for the shadow trial. SEWA's documentation pack (SEWA-AI-DOC-01, SEWA-AI-DOC-12) and the NHS Trust Pack v2.0 provide the governance, safety, and procurement frameworks needed to evaluate and join the programme.
